paras: The La Joya shooting and manhunt was a December 1880 episode in New Mexico Territory in which a storekeeper shot four Mexican men at La Joya and a sheriff's posse, later reported as thirty men, hunted him with open talk of lynching. Wire reports named the fugitive as Charles Bonssill or Bonsail, but the Las Vegas Morning Gazette later said the shooter was a Texan, John B. Hall, who escaped the country and so avoided a lynching.

La Joya was described as a Mexican town in the Rio Grande valley, 170 miles below Las Vegas, where the accused had recently opened a store. According to the sheriff's account printed in Las Vegas, the storekeeper went to the home of a man named Barcia on Monday night, December 13, and made an 'improper overture' to a young woman there, after which her brother ordered him out of the house.

In the quarrel that followed he opened fire, killing the brothers Jesus Maria and Jose Ignacio Barcia and wounding Sylvestre Esquibel and Manuel Terrara, both thought to be mortally hurt. At 4:45 the next morning fifteen mounted, armed men led by the sheriff stopped the northbound express at La Joya station, and the sheriff and one deputy searched the cars without finding him.

A Santa Fe dispatch the same day reported that thirty men were 'scouring the country' for the fugitive, and the Chicago Times' Santa Fe correspondent wrote that 'He will be lynched if caught.' The Gazette itself predicted he would be 'strung up at once' because nothing but 'a hearing before Judge Lynch' would satisfy the excited people.

On December 24 the Gazette reported that Charles Bonsall, whom it called a highly respected Albuquerque man, had been named by mistake, as had John Putney, the name it first printed. It identified the shooter as John B. Hall, agent at La Joya for Z. Staab of Santa Fe, and said he 'succeed ed in getting out of ihe country thus escaping a lynching.' No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached distant papers as a terse wire item: California and Nebraska dailies ran the Santa Fe dispatch on December 16, with the place garbled as 'La Java' or 'Lajava' and, in the Omaha Daily Bee, moved to Santa Fe itself. A week later Wisconsin weeklies listed it under 'CRIME.' as 'A lynching party of thirty men' near 'La Jara' hunting 'Charles Bonssill' for an 'affray about a lady'.

The Highland Weekly News of Ohio printed the fullest wire version on December 30, naming the victims and judging the fugitive's 'chances for immediate lynching' to be 'more than good'. German-language papers in Columbus and Baltimore turned it into a love story about John Putney and Maria Barela, set on the California-Mexican border, in January and February 1881. None of these reports describes any party as Black; the papers set 'a young American' against the 'Mexicans' he shot.

The shooter's name changed from report to report, from Bonssill or Bonsail in the wire, to Putney in the first Gazette account, to Hall in its correction, which as the latest local report is the strongest evidence. The cause also differs: early reports blamed a quarrel over a young woman, while the Gazette's correction relayed a claim that rival traders, envious of Hall's business, provoked the fight to drive him out.

bases: A shooting of four Mexican men by a man the papers call 'a young American' or 'a Texan', followed by a sheriff's posse and a body of thirty men hunting him with talk of lynching; no capture or killing by the pursuers is reported (A1, A2, A10).

Fifteen to thirty men hunted the accused and papers predicted he would be lynched if caught, but the Las Vegas Gazette reported that he got out of the country 'thus escaping a lynching'; no one was killed by the pursuers (A1, A2, A10).
The local Las Vegas Gazette and independent Santa Fe wire dispatches agree on the double killing at La Joya and the hunt by thirty men, though they disagree on the shooter's name (A1, A2, A5, A10).

accounts.label: Sheriff's story via Las Vegas Gazette
accounts.gist: Putney made improper overtures to a young girl at the Barcia house, was ordered out, and opened fire, killing two brothers and wounding two men; a sheriff's band hunted him.

accounts.label: Santa Fe wire
accounts.gist: Charles Bonsail (variously spelled) killed two Mexicans and wounded two in a difficulty about a Mexican girl; thirty men were hunting him and he would be lynched if caught.

accounts.label: Las Vegas Gazette correction
accounts.gist: The shooter was John B. Hall, a Texan trader; it was claimed envious rival traders provoked the quarrel; Hall escaped the country.

accounts.label: German-language romance
accounts.gist: Putney, engaged to Maria Barela, was caught with her by her brothers and shot them and three neighbors; thirty residents pursued him.

framing.detail: Midwestern weeklies ran a one-sentence 'CRIME.' item on 'A lynching party of thirty men' without comment.
The Las Vegas Gazette called the shooting 'cold blooded murder' and expected the man to be 'strung up at once', later reporting his escape from 'a lynching' without disapproval or approval.
German-language papers recast it as a love story ending in a 'fünffachen Morde'.
